content.title: About
content.content: Ice cream is a frozen dessert made from milk, cream, sugar, and flavorings. It may contain eggs, fruit, nuts, chocolate, and other mix‑ins. Traditionally it is served as scoops in cones, cups, or as a soft‑serve product.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest ice cream‑like desserts were created in China over 2,000 years ago using snow and milk.
Soft‑serve ice cream became popular in the United States in the 1930s thanks to its creamy texture.
The world’s most expensive ice cream flavor – “gold” with edible gold leaf – costs over $1,000 per serving.
Japan offers soy‑milk based ice cream, known as “soy ice cream,” suitable for vegans.
Ice cream is often used in culinary shows as a “cold” element to create contrasting textures.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base provides calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cream and milk supply vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Ice cream offers a fast source of calories, useful for replenishing energy after exercise when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Mood boost
items.content: Eating ice cream can trigger endorphin release, improving mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large portions can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People who are lactose intolerant may experience discomfort after consuming traditional ice cream.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey can cause reactions when eating ice cream.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some industrial ice creams may contain trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve ice cream as scoops in waffle cones, cups, in dessert suﬂés, or use it as a base for milkshakes. Add fruit, nuts, sauces, and sprinkles to diversify flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ice cream in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, consume within 1–2 weeks to prevent crystallization and flavor loss.

content.title: About
content.content: Iced Coffee, brewed is a cold coffee drink made by brewing ground coffee with hot water and then chilling it. The beverage retains the bright aroma of fresh coffee, a refreshing taste, and a moderate bitterness. It is often served over ice and may be complemented with milk, cream, or sweeteners.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cold brewed coffee recipe appeared in Japan in the early 20th century.
Unlike cold brew, Iced Coffee is brewed with hot water, preserving a brighter acidity and aroma.
Because the coffee is served over ice, a stronger brew is usually used to maintain flavor.
Iced Coffee gained widespread popularity in the United States during the 1990s alongside the rise of fast‑food chains.

items.title: Stimulating effect
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, enhancing alertness and reducing fatigue.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals and may lower the risk of certain diseases.

items.title: Metabolism boost
items.content: Caffeine can increase metabolic rate and aid in calorie burning.

items.title: Improved endurance
items.content: Caffeine promotes the use of fat as an energy source, beneficial for prolonged exercise.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine consumption.

items.title: High acidity
items.content: The acidity of coffee can irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: When sweeteners or syrups are added, the drink’s calorie content rises sharply.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Iced Coffee in a glass over ice; optionally add milk, cream, plant‑based milk, or a sweetener. Flavor with vanilla, caramel, or cinnamon if desired. For a richer taste, use a double shot of ground coffee.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared iced coffee in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24‑48 hours. Over longer storage the flavor may become more bitter, so it is best to brew in batches.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut butter is a paste made by grinding roasted or raw peanuts. The lower‑sodium version contains only 0.2 g of salt per 100 g, making it a better choice for those watching their sodium intake. It has a creamy texture, rich nutty flavor, and a faint hint of sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanut butter became a staple among American athletes in the 1960s as a quick source of energy.
Reduced sodium is achieved by using a small amount of sea salt instead of regular table salt.
Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts, so some people with tree‑nut allergies can tolerate peanut butter.
Over 200 million jars of peanut butter are sold annually in the United States.
Peanut butter can contain up to 50 % heart‑healthy monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One tablespoon (≈ 16 g) provides about 4 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids help promote heart health and lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Lower sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt helps control blood pressure and reduces kidney strain.

items.title: Provides magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter can trigger severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: One tablespoon contains roughly 95 kcal, so portion control is important.

items.title: Aflatoxin risk
items.content: Poor‑quality peanuts may be contaminated with aflatoxins, which are carcinogenic; choose reputable brands.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Some varieties contain a small amount of sugar; check the label if you monitor sugar intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread peanut butter on toast, stir into smoothies, use in sauces, bake with it, or add to oatmeal and yogurt. For a softer spread, gently warm it before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a tightly sealed jar in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, refrigerate to slow fat oxidation. Discard if it develops a rancid smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Pomegranate (Punica granatum) is a fruit-bearing shrub native to warm regions. Raw pomegranate arils have a juicy, slightly tart‑sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. They are eaten fresh, added to salads, desserts, juices, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pomegranate is one of the oldest cultivated plants, with cultivation dating back over 5,000 years in Persia.
Each pomegranate contains anywhere from 200 to 1,400 seeds surrounded by juicy arils.
Pomegranate juice was used in ancient rituals as a symbol of immortality and fertility.
The peel and leaves possess antioxidant properties and are used in traditional medicine.
Pomegranate trees can live for more than 200 years.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Pomegranate is high in polyphenols such as punicalagin, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Studies suggest regular consumption of pomegranate juice may help lower blood pressure and improve endothelial function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in pomegranate boosts immunity and supports collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in the arils aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Promotes skin health
items.content: Antioxidants and vitamin C help protect skin from premature aging.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pomegranate, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Pomegranate juice can enhance the effects of certain drugs, such as statins and anticoagulants.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw pomegranate arils can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, yogurt, oatmeal, smoothies, and desserts. Juice can be pressed manually or with a juicer. For a softer texture, soak the arils briefly in warm water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pomegranates in a cool, dry place at 5‑10 °C, in a paper bag or breathable basket. For longer storage (over 2‑3 weeks) keep them in the refrigerator. Avoid airtight plastic bags to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. The drumstick is the thigh portion with the lower part of the leg. Roasted turkey drumstick with the skin on retains juiciness and flavor, while the skin adds a crispy crust and contains beneficial fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey skin is rich in collagen, which supports skin, hair, and joint health.
Roasting with the skin helps lock moisture inside the meat, making it more tender.
Turkey provides all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
In traditional American cuisine, roasted turkey drumsticks are often served with cranberry sauce.
Turkey contains more iron than chicken, which helps prevent anemia.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: A turkey drumstick supplies about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Moderate fat content (with skin)
items.content: Even with the skin, the overall fat level remains moderate, and most fats are monounsaturated and polyunsaturated.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey is a good source of niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: Iron enhances oxygen transport, while zinc supports immunity and wound healing.

items.title: Collagen from the skin
items.content: The skin contains collagen that may benefit joint and skin health.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat, including turkey.

items.title: Sodium in prepared products
items.content: Ready‑to‑eat roasted drumsticks are often seasoned with salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor salmonella or campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Those with gout should limit excessive consumption, as purines can trigger attacks.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted turkey drumsticks can be served as a main dish, sliced for salads, sandwiches, or added to soups. The skin can be eaten as a crunchy snack or removed according to preference.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked drumsticks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a bag at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Waffle plain (3087) is a crisp, light dessert made from a batter of wheat flour, eggs, sugar, and butter. It has a golden crust and a soft interior, suitable as a snack on its own or as a base for sweet toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Waffles originated in medieval Europe and quickly became popular due to their simple preparation.
Traditional waffles are baked in special iron or metal grids that create a characteristic pattern.
Waffle plain (3087) contains no added flavors, making it a versatile base for a variety of toppings.
Waffles are often served with fruit, whipped cream, ice cream, or chocolate sauce.
There are many regional waffle variations that differ in thickness and texture.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Waffle provides a quick source of energy thanks to its carbohydrate content.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs in the batter supply a modest amount of both animal and plant protein.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour offers B1, B2, and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Plain waffle contains less fat than many other baked goods when no extra butter is added to the batter.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Its light texture makes it easy to digest, suitable for children and older adults.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Waffle contains wheat flour, so it may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugar increases calorie count and may be unsuitable for diabetics.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Consuming large amounts can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar levels.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: When buying pre‑made waffles, check for preservatives and artificial flavorings.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Waffles can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, split in half and spread with butter, jam, honey, or nut butter. They also pair well with fresh fruit, berries, ice cream, and chocolate sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store waffles in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to maintain crispness. Before eating, check for any mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: White beans are dried beans (commonly cannellini or navy varieties) to which a plant oil has been added to improve flavor and texture. The beans are rich in protein, complex carbohydrates and dietary fiber, while the added fat raises their energy content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White beans are a staple in Mediterranean and Latin American cuisines.
Dried beans can be stored for 2–3 years when kept in a cool, dry place.
Adding fat helps preserve aroma during long-term storage.
Beans are a good source of iron, especially for vegetarian diets.
Proper soaking reduces cooking time and improves digestibility.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked beans provides about 15 g of protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High dietary fiber content
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes satiety.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Beans release glucose slowly, providing steady energy throughout the day.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Contains iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and B‑vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Added plant fat
items.content: The oil enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and makes the dish more satisfying.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting mitigate this.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Added fat increases calories, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Potential gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause flatulence; proper soaking and cooking reduce this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak the dried beans in water for at least 6–8 hours, then boil until tender (about 45 minutes). Cooked beans can be added to soups, stews, salads, purees, or used as a base for vegetarian patties. The added fat makes them especially flavorful when sautéed or baked.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth and quality loss.
